result:
The low tide at Cairn’s Reach does not reveal shells or stranded kelp; it reveals the debris of things that almost happened. 

Locals call the flat expanse of gray silt *the Ledger*. Twice a day, the water pulls back three miles into the northern gray mist, leaving behind a damp, shimmering plain littered with fragments. Most people ignore it. If you spend your life looking down at the silt, you will eventually find a key to a door that was never built, or a photograph of two people who looked at each other across a crowded carriage in 1974 and then turned away. It makes for poor sleeping.

I work as a sifter. It is not an official municipal title, but the town council leaves an envelope of small bills on my porch at the end of each month because I keep the heavier residues from choking the harbor mouth. 

My kit is simple: high rubber boots, a pair of wooden tongs, and a zinc-lined canvas bucket. Metal tongs bruise the softer specimens; iron shears them clean through. If you cut an unsaid sentence in half, both pieces will thrash in the mud like severed eels until the next tide drowns them. It is better to lift them whole.

The morning after a gale is always the heaviest. I stepped down from the stone quay around six, the air sharp with iodine and wet coal. The wind had died, leaving the bay so still that the distant bell-buoy sounded like a spoon tapping the rim of a tea saucer. 

Within ten yards of the high-water mark, I found a cluster of small intentions. They look like blown glass when the light hits them right—pale, milky bubbles, no larger than plum stones, with a slight oily iridescence. I picked one up with the tongs. It was cold, vibrating faintly against the ash-wood handles. Through the curved skin of it, I could see an afternoon light: someone had meant to walk up a hill on a Tuesday to see if the foxglove was blooming. They had put their boots on, tied the laces, and then the kettle had whistled, or someone had knocked on the back door, and the hill had gone unclimbed. A harmless thing. I dropped it into the bucket, where it settled with a dry clink.

Further out, near the spine of the black reef, the silt gives up the heavier weights. 

These are the apologies that sat on the tongue until the train pulled away; the third verses of songs abandoned because the rhyming word felt too plain; the business ventures sketched on the backs of menus that dissolved in the wash. They do not look like glass. They look like lead sinkers, or knotty roots of bog-oak, dark and damp and smelling faintly of turned earth.

I knelt by a deep runnel where the water was still draining seaward. Half-buried in the mud was a long, pale strip, like a parchment ribbon. When I washed it clean in the outflow, the script became visible—not letters, precisely, but the cadence of an argument that never took place. It had the bitter, electrical tang of a grievance carefully tended in silence for twenty years, polished in private until its corners were razor-sharp, only for the other party to die peacefully in their sleep on an ordinary Thursday. 

There is a great deal of sorrow in the Ledger, but it is not dramatic sorrow. It is the dull, heavy weight of the conditional tense: *would have, could have, might have been.* 

Around noon, the sun came through as a pale silver disk behind the clouds, casting no shadows. I sat down on an overturned crate—an actual crate, pine and barnacles, drifted down from the timber wharves—and ate a boiled egg and two cold potatoes sprinkled with coarse salt. Out past the two-mile mark, the silt turns black and soft. No one goes there. If you sink past your knees in the outer mud, the pull is not gravitational; it is mnemonic. You begin to remember things that occurred to your grandfather’s cousins: their unpaid debts, their sudden terrors in the dark, their forgotten dreams of crossing the plains. A man could drown in twenty inches of water out there, held fast by the sheer density of strangers' regrets.

Before turning back, I saw something caught on an iron stake that marked the old oyster beds. 

It was neither glass nor lead. It fluttered in the light breeze like a moth’s wing, translucent and pale amber. I approached it cautiously, my boots sucking in the mud with heavy, wet gasps. 

I reached out with the tongs, but as the wood neared the amber scrap, the tips began to smoke faintly. I put the tools away, pulled off my leather work-glove, and touched it with my bare fingers.

It was warm. 

The moment skin met skin—for that is what it felt like, dried and salted parchment skin—a sound rose up through my collarbones. It was the sound of a front door closing softly in late autumn, followed by the specific, dry click of a latch falling home. It was mine.

I had forgotten that I had left it here. Forty years ago, when the railway still ran all the way to the pierhead, I had stood on the platform with a ticket to the capital tucked into the band of my hat. I had stood there through three announcements, watching the steam curl around the wheels of the engine, listening to the porter shout the names of stations I had only ever seen on maps. And then I had walked away. I had told myself I was only going for tobacco. I had walked down the ramp, past the salt-houses, out onto the marshes, and never went back.

I held the small amber fragment in my palm. It didn't weigh more than a dry beech leaf. 

I could take it home. I could drop it into a jar of sweet oil on the mantelpiece, where it would glow like an ember through the winter evenings, reminding me of the life that had waited for me on the other side of the mountains—the rooms I hadn't rented, the books I hadn't read, the strangers who would have become my companions.

The sea-horn sounded from the lightship, three low blasts: the tide had turned. 

The water was already rushing back across the flats, faster than a horse can trot, a thin, silver sheet running before the white froth of the swell. The Ledger was closing for the day.

I looked down at the amber leaf in my hand. It was beautiful, but it was dead. It was the shape of an absence, nothing more.

I knelt, set it gently back onto the black mud, and let the first cold tongue of the incoming tide take it away.
